name: ucspi-tcp
desc: Tools for building TCP client-server applications
why: D. J. Bernstein's tcpserver and tcpclient toolkit is a sharp, strange door into how TCP servers are built from the shell.

brief.what_it_is: ucspi-tcp is a set of small command-line UNIX tools by D. J. Bernstein for building TCP client-server applications. tcpserver listens on a host and port and, for each incoming connection, runs a program of your choice with the network on its stdin and stdout, plus environment variables describing the local and remote host names, IP addresses and ports. tcpclient makes an outgoing TCP connection and runs a program the same way. The package also ships sample clients built on tcpclient (who@, date@, finger@, http@, tcpcat, mconnect), plus recordio for logging a server's input and output, and rules tools (tcprules, tcprulescheck) that compile access-control rules into a cdb hash file.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a replacement for inetd, which the author says is unreliable under high loads, has no effective resource management, and has a listen() backlog that is typically only 5 or 10. The stated aim is easy-to-use command-line TCP tools with a concurrency limit and fast, hashed access control.
brief.how_it_works: For each accepted connection, tcpserver forks the program given as prog, wiring descriptor 0 to read from the network and descriptor 1 to write to it. It defers accepting new connections once the concurrency limit (default 40, set with -c) is reached. Access rules compiled by tcprules into a cdb file (passed with -x) can reject sources or set environment variables, and can be recompiled while the server runs.

commands_seen.context: Install step: decompress the downloaded 0.88 tarball (the page lists this as the latest published package).
Install step: unpack the source tree.
Install step: enter the unpacked source directory.
Install step: compile the ucspi-tcp programs.
Install step, run as root: installs the programs under /usr/local and runs checks.

Interface summary from the tcpserver page: opts are getopt-style options, host is an IP or host name (0 for any local address), port is a name or number (0 picks a free port), and prog is the program to run per connection.
Option: cap simultaneous connections at n; new connections are deferred while n copies of prog are running. Default 40.
Option: follow access rules and environment settings compiled into cdb by tcprules; rules can be rerun while tcpserver runs.
Option: write banner to the client immediately on connect, to cut latency for protocols where the client waits for a greeting.
Option: give up on the TCPREMOTEINFO lookup after n seconds (default 26).

brief.install_notes: UNIX only. Download the ucspi-tcp package (latest listed as ucspi-tcp-0.88.tar.gz), unpack, run make, then as root run make setup check to install under /usr/local. The install page asks users who succeed to report it by piping their name and the SYSDEPS file to a mailing list address (djb-sysdeps@cr.yp.to). No accounts, runtimes or hardware are mentioned. Homebrew users get a packaged version with no brew-specific caveats recorded.
brief.standout: Access control is compiled into a cdb hash so the lookup stays fast even with thousands of host rules, and the tool passes connection metadata to an ordinary program through environment variables instead of requiring a server-side plugin model. The tool is a small, Unix-style alternative to inetd, xinetd, netcat and netpipes.
brief.status: Unknown. The homepage and install page are static pages on cr.yp.to with no release date or changelog date visible in what I read. The latest package named is 0.88. I did not check the repository or Homebrew for recent commits.
brief.caveats: Works only under UNIX, per the install page. The install page says the software comes with NO WARRANTY. Installing requires root for make setup check. The homepage did not state a license in the text I read. The tcpserver docs say that to avoid DNS loops, servers on TCP port 53 and 113 must use certain -H, -l and -R options. The homepage's scout note calls it strange, which is editorial; the page itself is terse and assumes Unix background.

judge.reason: Its unusual Unix model turns each TCP connection into stdin/stdout for an ordinary program, with connection metadata in the environment and live-compiled access rules.

entry.title: ucspi-tcp
entry.tldr: D. J. Bernstein's tcpserver and tcpclient turn any program that reads stdin and writes stdout into a TCP server or client, no socket code needed.
entry.deeper_look:
ucspi-tcp is a set of small Unix tools for building TCP client-server applications. `tcpserver` listens on a host and port. For each incoming connection it forks a program you name, with descriptor 0 reading from the network and descriptor 1 writing to it. Details about the connection arrive as environment variables: local and remote host names, IP addresses and ports. `tcpclient` does the mirror image, making an outgoing connection and running a program wired to it the same way.

The package exists as a replacement for inetd. The homepage states it plainly: "inetd is unreliable under high loads." It also says inetd has no effective resource management and a listen() backlog that is typically only 5 or 10. In response, tcpserver has a concurrency limit (default 40, set with `-c`) that defers new connections instead of running the machine out of processes and memory.

The idea underneath is that a network service can be an ordinary program. It does not link a networking library or implement a plugin interface. It reads input, writes output, and looks at its environment. Access control follows the same spirit. `tcprules` compiles allow and deny rules into a cdb hash file, so lookups stay fast with thousands of rules, and the rules can be recompiled while the server runs.

The bundled extras are small sample clients built on tcpclient (`who@`, `date@`, `finger@`, `http@`, `tcpcat`, `mconnect`), plus `recordio`, which logs what a server's input and output looked like. Together they make a compact way to see what a TCP conversation is made of.
entry.install:
brew install ucspi-tcp
# Unix only. Building from source instead: unpack ucspi-tcp-0.88, run make, then as root run make setup check (installs under /usr/local).

try_this.what_happens: Prints usage for tcpserver, whose form is tcpserver opts host port prog. It is a quick look at the options before you wire up a first service.
Caps simultaneous connections at n. New connections wait while n copies of your program are running. The default is 40.
Prints usage for tcpclient, the outgoing-connection counterpart that runs a program attached to the socket.

entry.whats_unique: Connection metadata reaches an ordinary program through environment variables, and access rules compile into a cdb hash that can be swapped while the server runs. It is a small, Unix-style alternative to inetd, xinetd, netcat and netpipes.
entry.caveats: The pages carry no visible release date and the latest package named is 0.88, so treat it as old, finished software. The docs are terse and assume Unix background.
